blocks.text: On July 23, 1985, Commodore introduced its Amiga 1000 computer. And let’s just say the world wasn’t ready for it yet. Dave Haynie, a Commodore engineer who worked on the later models, has said there was no such thing as a 1980s computer. There were 1970s computers and 1990s computers, and it was the Amiga that dragged the rest of the industry into the 1990s.

It is not hyperbole to say the Amiga 1000 was 10 years ahead of its time. Its custom chipset had color graphics with up to 4,096 colors, stereo sound, a graphical user interface. Its operating system had full preemptive multitasking. The combination of the chipset and the operating system meant it could run on a Motorola 68000 CPU clocked at 7.14 megahertz and 256 KB of RAM. And it could boot and run off a single floppy drive. Amiga demonstrated it in January 1984, when the chips existed only as prototype circuit boards. By the end of 1985, it was a shipping product.
Realistically, an ideal configuration had dual floppy drives and 512k of RAM, and a megabyte was a lot nicer.

But dual floppies and a meg of RAM wasn’t an outlandish machine in 1985, and in that configuration, it was smooth and pleasant to use. Commodore commissioned artist Andy Warhol to demonstrate it by using it to create digital art to show off its capabilities.
Multitasking: The Amiga 1000’s secret

Graphical user interfaces weren’t exactly new in the summer of 1985. Apple had introduced the Macintosh about a year and a half earlier, and the Lisa predated even that by a nearly a year. Atari released its ST computer three months before the Amiga, and the ST also had a graphical operating system with a mouse and color.

It was multitasking that put the Amiga on the map. And it wasn’t the cooperative multitasking that Windows 3.0 and 3.1 did or Apple System 7 did. It was full preemptive multitasking like Windows 95. The only thing Windows NT did that the Amiga didn’t was memory protection.
The Amiga’s operating system wasn’t based on Unix and it certainly wasn’t based on Windows NT. Its direct ancestor was an operating system called TRIPOS that originated at Cambridge University.

Adding memory protection would have been a nice touch, but the additional required hardware would have increased costs. And the Amiga at its debut was not exactly inexpensive. The base system cost $1,295 without a monitor. A color monitor, which you definitely wanted, cost another $300. Add the additional memory and a second floppy drive for another $150 to $200 each, and you soon learned the Amiga you really wanted was more like a $2,000 computer. Living in the future was expensive, but compared to the $2,495 Apple wanted for a less capable machine, the price wasn’t unreasonable.
Living with an Amiga

I’m not sure I even saw an Amiga in person until 1987, but I knew just from reading about it that I wanted one. I wasn’t able to make it happen until 1991, so I was pretty late to the game. But even in 1991, an Amiga felt like living in the future. I could load several programs and switch between them effortlessly, with the only limit being the amount of memory I had. I could connect to a BBS with a terminal program, start a download, then switch it to the background, fire up a word processor, and do my homework while the download was happening. In some cases, I could even fire up a game and play a game while a download happened in the background. I could download stuff while I played Civilization, which was pretty great.

Initially, the Amiga had a reputation for being unstable. But that was largely because early Amiga software wasn’t very well written. Amiga software was prone to ask for resources, and assume the resources were available. Instead of failing gracefully if the resources it asked for weren’t available, it would simply allocate them, and cause a guru meditation, the Amiga equivalent of a blue screen of death or kernel panic. Except it was red, not blue.

But it wasn’t long before the software developers learned how to write code that behaved in this brave new world. Certainly by the time I was in the scene in 1991, the software generally behaved very well. When I bought a Windows PC in 1994, it felt like a serious downgrade. If I treated it like an Amiga and launched a terminal program, connected to a BBS, started download, and then switched over to Microsoft Word, it didn’t always work reliably. More often than not it was fine. But something would crash often enough to make me hesitate doing something I took for granted on an Amiga.
People ask me all the time when PCs caught up. It didn’t happen all at once. And it wasn’t until 1995 that all the pieces were there.
Why the Amiga makes me mad

And that’s why I almost everything about the Amiga makes me mad. With a good product marketing team behind it, it would have been the greatest computer of all time. When anyone asks its engineers why they built it, they tell you things like they wanted to build the very best computer that they could with the technology that was available to them at the time. That’s how engineers think, so it’s a perfectly good answer, engineer to engineer. But that answer doesn’t sell. You have to come up with something about wanting to change the world. And you have to word it in a way that sounds believable if you are going to attract a mass audience. Apple does that very well. Microsoft was never as good at it, but they were better at it than Commodore.

Commodore didn’t have a Steve Jobs or even a Steve Ballmer. They had an oligarch named Irving Gould who was only interested in looting as much from the company as possible as he ran it into the ground. It is a testament to the quality of the product Commodore had that it took him a decade to do it after Jack Tramiel left the company and left him unchecked to rob it blind.

Commodore ran a few ads, but it was clear from their advertising they had no idea what they were selling. The most effective marketers were the people who bought one. Sit down for an hour with an Amiga and someone who knew how to use it, and you’d want one too. But there weren’t enough of us to sustain the platform or the company.
How the Amiga 1000 and its successors were like a kick in the face

Commodore went bankrupt less than 9 years after introducing the first Amiga. And the company they sold it to went out of business about 15 months after buying it. So instead of getting the greatest computer of all time, it felt like we were getting kicked in the face repeatedly. And then we tried to switch to Apple or Microsoft, and waiting years for them to catch up felt like getting kicked in the face by two people.

If you missed out on it, it sounds like I’m being overdramatic. I get it. Nobody knows exactly how many people got to experience it. In the end Commodore sold around 4.91 million Amigas, but at least in the United States, Amiga owners were prone to buy more than one. That makes it hard to say how many distinct owners the machine had. But the people who owned one and lived in the future waiting for the rest of the world to catch up know exactly what I’m talking about.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

translations: 1985年7月23日，Commodore 推出了 Amiga 1000 计算机。可以说，当时的世界还没准备好迎接它。参与过后续型号研发的 Commodore 工程师 Dave Haynie 曾表示，根本不存在所谓的80年代计算机。只有70年代的计算机和90年代的计算机，正是 Amiga 将整个行业的其他产品拖入了90年代。

说 Amiga 1000 领先时代10年绝非夸张。其定制芯片组支持最高4096色的彩色图形、立体声以及图形用户界面。它的操作系统具备完全的抢占式多任务处理能力。芯片组与操作系统的结合意味着它可以在主频为7.14兆赫兹的 Motorola 68000 CPU 和 256 KB 的 RAM 上运行。而且它只需单个软驱即可启动和运行。Amiga 在1984年1月进行了演示，当时芯片还只是原型电路板。到1985年底，它已成为上市销售的产品。
现实中，理想的配置是双软驱 512k RAM，而 1MB 的内存则更好。
但在1985年，双软驱和 1MB 的 RAM 并不算什么离奇的机器，在这种配置下，它的使用体验流畅且令人愉悦。Commodore 委托艺术家 Andy Warhol 通过使用它创作数字艺术来展示其功能，以炫耀其能力。
多任务处理：Amiga 1000 的秘密
在1985年夏天，图形用户界面已不算什么新鲜事物。Apple 在大约一年半前推出了 Macintosh，而 Lisa 甚至比那还要早近一年。Atari 在 Amiga 之前三个月发布了其 ST 计算机，ST 同样配备了带鼠标和彩色的图形操作系统。
正是多任务处理让 Amiga 声名鹊起。而且它不是 Windows 3.0 和 3.1 或 Apple System 7 所采用的那种协作式多任务处理。它是像 Windows 95 一样的完全抢占式多任务处理。Windows NT 做到了而 Amiga 没有做到的唯一一点是内存保护。
Amiga 的操作系统不是基于 Unix 的，当然也不是基于 Windows NT 的。它的直接前身是一个名为 TRIPOS 的操作系统，起源于剑桥大学。

增加内存保护会是个不错的点缀，但所需的额外硬件会增加成本。而且 Amiga 在初次亮相时并不便宜。不含显示器的基础系统售价为1295美元。你肯定想要的彩色显示器还要再花300美元。再加上额外内存和第二个软驱，每个又要150到200美元，你很快就会发现你真正想要的 Amiga 更像是一台2000美元的计算机。生活在未来是昂贵的，但与 Apple 为一台性能较弱的机器索要的2495美元相比，这个价格并非不合理。
与 Amiga 共同生活

我不确定自己在1987年之前是否亲眼见过 Amiga，但仅仅从阅读相关文章我就知道我想要一台。直到1991年我才如愿以偿，所以我入局相当晚了。但即使在1991年，Amiga 也让人感觉像生活在未来。我可以加载多个程序并在它们之间毫不费力地切换，唯一的限制是我的内存大小。我可以用终端程序连接到 BBS，开始下载，然后将其切换到后台，启动文字处理软件，在下载的同时做我的作业。在某些情况下，我甚至可以在后台下载时启动并玩游戏。我可以一边玩《文明》一边下载东西，这真是太棒了。
起初，Amiga 有着不稳定的坏名声。但这主要是因为早期的 Amiga 软件写得不太好。Amiga 软件习惯于请求资源，并假定资源总是可用的。如果请求的资源不可用，它不会优雅地报错，而是直接分配，从而引发“Guru Meditation”（大师冥想）错误——这是 Amiga 相当于蓝屏死机或内核崩溃的报错机制。只不过它是红色的，而不是蓝色的。

但没过多久，软件开发者就学会了如何在这个美丽新世界中编写行为规范的代码。当然，到了1991年我进入这个圈子时，软件的运行通常已经非常稳定了。当我在1994年买了一台 Windows PC 时，感觉像是严重的降级。如果我像对待 Amiga 那样，启动终端程序，连接到 BBS，开始下载，然后切换到 Microsoft Word，它并不总是能可靠地运行。大多数时候是没问题的。但总有些东西会时不时崩溃，让我对在 Amiga 上习以为常的操作产生犹豫。
人们总是问我 PC 是什么时候赶上来的。这并不是一蹴而就的。直到1995年，所有的拼图才终于凑齐。
为什么 Amiga 让我生气

这就是为什么 Amiga 的几乎一切都让我感到生气。如果背后有一个优秀的产品营销团队，它本可以成为有史以来最伟大的计算机。当任何人问它的工程师为什么要制造它时，他们会告诉你，他们想用当时可用的技术制造出最好的计算机。这就是工程师的思维方式，所以从工程师到工程师的角度来看，这是一个非常好的回答。但这个回答卖不动。你必须想出一些关于想要改变世界的东西。而且，如果你想吸引大众，你必须用一种听起来令人信服的方式来表达。Apple 在这方面做得非常好。Microsoft 从来没有这么擅长，但他们比 Commodore 强。
Commodore 没有 Steve Jobs，甚至连 Steve Ballmer 都没有。他们有一个名叫 Irving Gould 的寡头，他唯一感兴趣的就是在公司被他搞垮的同时尽可能多地中饱私囊。在 Jack Tramiel 离开公司并让他肆无忌惮地洗劫公司之后，他竟然花了十年时间才把公司搞垮，这足以证明 Commodore 产品的质量有多高。
Commodore 做过一些广告，但从他们的广告中可以明显看出，他们根本不知道自己在卖什么。最有效的营销人员是那些购买了它的人。和一台 Amiga 以及一个知道如何使用它的人坐上一个小时，你也会想要一台。但我们这样的人还不够多，不足以维持这个平台或这家公司。
Amiga 1000 及其后续产品如何像是一记耳光
Commodore 在推出第一台 Amiga 后不到9年就破产了。而他们把公司卖给的买家在收购约15个月后也倒闭了。因此，我们没有得到有史以来最伟大的计算机，反而感觉像是被反复扇耳光。然后我们试图转向 Apple 或 Microsoft，而等待他们花几年时间才赶上来的感觉，就像是同时被两个人扇耳光。
如果你错过了它，听起来我可能有些夸张。我理解。没人确切知道有多少人体验过它。最终Commodore售出了约491万台Amiga，但至少在美国，Amiga用户往往会购买不止一台。这使得很难说清这台机器究竟有多少独立用户。但那些拥有它、超前于时代生活并等待着世界其他地方赶上的人，完全明白我在说什么。
David Farquhar是一名计算机安全专家、企业家和作家。自1991年起，他便从事专业的计算机写作，因此当复古计算机还是新事物时，他就在撰写关于它们的内容了。他自1994年起从事专业的IT工作，并自2013年起专注于漏洞管理。他拥有Security+和CISSP认证。如今，他每周撰写五篇博客，主要涵盖1975年至2000年期间的复古计算机和复古游戏。

blocks.text: Is creatine a weird steroid-like hormone or drug?

No. Creatine is a nutrient. Most omnivores eat a gram or two per day from meat. Your body also synthesizes a gram or two per day. You need creatine to deliver energy inside of cells. It is normal and non-weird.
Does creatine increase testosterone?

Unlikely. This concern comes from one study in 2009 on 16 male rugby players.1 But that study is considered extremely suspect. There have been at least twelve other studies that all found no change or physiologically irrelevant changes. Beyond that, it’s implausible that creatine would increase testosterone, because we know what creatine does and it has nothing to do with hormones.
Does creatine make you go bald?
No. Or, rather:
No study ever reported that.
One study reported the opposite.
There is no mechanistic reason to think that would happen.
There are good mechanistic reasons to think that would not happen.

These rumors all trace back to speculation built on top of that same single 2009 study. But that study is contradicted by later research, and anyway didn’t measure hair. Anything is possible, but as far as I can tell, it’s equally plausible that creatine would increase hair growth. And if you’re really worried about this: Are you going to stop eating meat?
Is creatine safe?
Probably. The International Society of Sports Nutrition says:

Available short and long-term studies in healthy and diseased populations, from infants to the elderly, at dosages ranging from 0.3 to 0.8 g/kg/day for up to 5 years have consistently shown that creatine supplementation poses no adverse health risks and may provide a number of health and performance benefits.

It’s been studied extensively, and no risks have been found. The way it works doesn’t suggest any risks. And supplementing a few grams per day doesn’t put you far outside the range that people get from normal food.
Does creatine make you stronger?

Yes. It’s very rare for a supplement to have such strong and consistent evidence. A widely-cited review says that short-term supplementation increases maximal power/strength by 5-15%. This in turn may increase the long-term gainz from strength-training exercise. Creatine also increases sprint performance by 1-5%. Though, there seems to be little if any benefit for endurance exercise like long-distance running.
But how does creatine make you stronger?
Before answering that, can I go on a rant about how muscles work?
…OK?
Great! Here’s how muscles work:
All cells have a molecule called ATP floating around inside, which they use for energy.
Muscle cells have proteins in them called myosin.
When ATP bumps into myosin, the myosin breaks the ATP down into ADP. This releases energy which is physically captured by the myosin as elastic strain.
When triggered by neurons, myosin releases that mechanical energy.
When you decide to move your arm, your brain triggers many muscle cells, carefully orchestrating the myosin twitches into large-scale movement.

Now, here’s something that’s crucial for our story: Very little energy is stored as ATP. Your body contains ~100 grams of ATP, representing ~10,000 joules of energy.2 But your body at rest burns ~100 watts. So you only store enough ATP to keep yourself alive for ~100 seconds. If you sprint, you could easily burn ~3000 watts, which would use all your stored ATP in ~3 seconds.

Through the magic of eating, you’re always making more ATP. Typically, your mitochondria recycle ~1 gram of ADP back into ATP per second, the same amount you need to stay alive.3 If you start running, your body can ramp that up to ~10 grams per second, though tricks like breathing faster and speeding up your heart.4 But it takes a minute or two for your mitochondria to really get cranking.5
So then why am I able to sprint for longer than three seconds?

Because creatine acts as an additional energy reservoir, coupled to the ATP reservoir. After you eat or synthesize creatine, 60% is converted into phosphocreatine. This is done by an enzyme that grabs a creatine molecule and an ATP molecule and moves a phosphate group between them. This “charges” the creatine into phosphocreatine and “discharges” the ATP into ADP.6

But if your ATP levels drop—e.g. because you’re running away from a tiger—those enzymes will run in reverse, meaning they “discharge” phosphocreatine into creatine and “charge” ADP back into ATP. This happens almost instantly, so that ATP and phosphocreatine deplete at the same rate.7

At rest, your muscles contain around 3-4 times as much phosphocreatine as ATP. So the “extra” energy storage in phosphocreatine is much larger than the “base” storage in ATP itself. That’s why you can sprint for ten seconds rather than just three seconds.
Does supplementing creatine increase creatine levels in muscle cells?
Yes. Typical levels are:
Vegetarian: 100 mmol / kg
Omnivore: 120 mmol / kg
Someone who supplements creatine: 140 mmol / kg

So, everything seems to add up. If you supplement creatine, you increase your levels by ~16.67%, implying ~12.5% more total short-term energy storage.8 That’s in line with the 5-15% increase in strength seen in creatine trials.9 It also seems to make sense that creatine trials find little benefit for endurance exercise. If you don’t have sudden bursts of activity, a larger short-term energy reservoir won’t really help you.
But isn’t this all very strange?

Well, I find it strange. All else equal, more strength is good. The body already knows how to make creatine. If you can just raise creatine levels and get more strength with no downsides, then shouldn’t evolution have done this already? Some variant of the Algernon argument would suggest that the fact that creatine works so well should be impossible.

You might think that higher creatine levels are bad somehow, and that’s why evolution didn’t make them higher. But that seems wrong. Creatine levels vary naturally based on what you eat. If higher levels were bad, evolution could have brought them down. But it doesn’t. It just lets them vary.

Often, evolution makes us “worse” to reduce our energy expenditures, because evolution hates it when we starve to death.10 But the body only spends 1-2 calories per day synthesizing creatine, and more creatine in muscle cells doesn’t have any significant metabolic cost.

I think the boring explanation is that for our evolutionary ancestors, modest increases in short-term strength just weren’t a big deal. We were exhaustion hunters, not 1-rep max deadlift hunters.11 Also, more creatine causes your muscle cells to draw in some extra water, which slightly increases energy usage for long-distance running.12 So, if you happened to get extra creatine from meat, great. If not, whatever. In the range where creatine fluctuates based on diet, I suspect creatine levels just didn’t have much impact on reproductive success.

Still, we must acknowledge that creatine is unusual. I wish we could tell our bodies, “Hey, we have access to unlimited amounts of food. Stop worrying about conserving energy and concentrate on being awesome.”  But we have very few ways to do that. As far as I can tell, the list of normal nutrients that have been proven to increase strength is: protein, creatine, beta-alanine, the end.
So creatine is special. And creatine makes you a little stronger. Does it make you a little smarter, too?
Is creatine used by the brain?

Yes. Most parts of the body don’t contain significant creatine. But the brain does, along with muscles, the heart, and testes. Neurons use it to play the same game muscles do with ATP and phosphate groups and so on.
How much creatine is in the brain?

Maybe half as much as in muscle. The number of interest here is the ratio of phosphocreatine to ATP, indicating how much phosphocreatine increases local energy storage. We saw above that in muscle, that ratio is 3 to 4. In the brain, the numbers are a little sketchy, but the ratio seems to be more like 1.5 to 2.13
But why? Why would the brain use creatine?

Good question! The brain doesn’t have bursts of energy usage like muscles do. Yes, the brain uses ~20% of all calories despite only making up ~2% of body mass. But the brain is unusual in that it needs all that energy just for basic housekeeping, and doesn’t ramp up with usage. Contrary to the common myth, thinking hard does not burn significantly more calories. (Demonstration: Start thinking hard, and watch as your heart rate does not increase.)
So muscles use creatine for sprints. But the brain doesn’t have sprints. So what the hell is the brain using creatine for?

The most common theory seems to go like this: Actually, muscles don’t just use creatine as an extra energy reservoir. They also use it to deliver energy inside of cells. You see, creatine diffuses faster than ATP inside of cells. So even with endurance exercise, creatine is still being used: Enzymes near the mitochondria use ATP to “charge” creatine into phosphocreatine and enzymes near myosin use that phosphocreatine to “recharge” ADP back into ATP. Even though the net change in creatine is zero, it helps “shuttle” energy from the mitochondria to the myosin.

Under this theory, what neurons and muscle cells share is that parts of the cell locally use a lot of energy, when they get triggered. So even though your brain doesn’t “sprint”, it still uses creatine to avoid local energy deficits.

There’s also experimental evidence that creatine is important for the brain. We’ve created genetically altered mice with brains that lack the enzymes needed to convert creatine to and from phosphocreatine. They display severely limited spatial learning and somewhat smaller brains.

Some humans also naturally have creatine deficiency. In some variants, people have trouble synthesizing creatine. This leads to lower levels throughout the body, including skeletal muscle where 95% of creatine lives. Nevertheless, the primary symptom is related to the brain, namely intellectual disability. Muscle weakness and seizures are also common. Other people have creatine transporter deficiency, meaning creatine can’t cross the blood-brain barrier. This leads to lower levels in the brain only. This leads again to intellectual disability and also often muscle weakness or seizures. (That muscle weakness is despite the fact that the muscle cells themselves have normal creatine levels.)14
So somehow, creatine is very important for the brain.
Does supplementing creatine increase creatine levels in the brain?
Probably, though likely less than in muscle.

Creatine can definitely cross the blood-brain barrier. However, the protein that helps it cross is not abundant, and there are some suggestions that it’s down-regulated with prolonged creatine consumption. The brain itself can synthesize some creatine, and this too might be down-regulated by prolonged consumption.

Of course, you can just give people creatine and see what happens to their brains. There have been around a dozen such studies. Most report increases between 3% and 10%, although a few report no change. However, because brains are hard to access, these studies rely on magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and some suggest that these measurements are unreliable.

In people who can’t synthesize creatine, oral supplementation seems to normalize levels in the brain. (Some cognitive impairment usually remains. One patient was diagnosed and began supplementing at three weeks of age and had no intellectual disability.) So supplementing can increase brain levels in some circumstances.
My best guess is that supplementing does usually increase levels in the brain, and that an increase of 3% to 10% is plausible. But the evidence isn’t particularly strong.
Why did people get interested in creatine having cognitive benefits?

Because of Rae et al. (2003). They took a group of 45 healthy vegetarian or vegan university students in Australia. They did a cross-over trial where half of people got 5 grams of creatine per day for six weeks, followed by a six-week wash-out period, followed by the other half of people getting creatine. Their results were amazing, with huge improvements on Raven’s matrices (RAPM) and backward digit span (BDS):

In their analysis, creatine increased BDS by 1.19 standard deviations, and RAPM by 1.76 standard deviations. If we convert those numbers to IQ points (where 1 standard deviation ←> 15 IQ points), that would mean increases of 17.85 and 26.4 IQ points, respectively. In both cases, the results were highly significant (p < 0.0001).
Does that replicate?

No. Following that paper various groups tried similar experiments but no one found such a large or statistically significant effect. After twenty years of inconclusive results, Sandkühler et al. (2023) set out to give a definitive reproduction. In my view, this is the highest-quality RCT ever done on the cognitive benefits of creatine.15 They largely borrowed the experimental design of Rae et al., although they did the experiment in Germany, used a larger sample of 123 people, used half non-vegetarians, and they dropped the wash-out period. Here are their main results:

(T1 shows test results at baseline. T2 shows results after six weeks of creatine or placebo. T3 shows the results after another six weeks, where the placebo group crossed over to creatine and vise versa.)

Overall, everyone got better over time, probably from practice. On backwards digit span, during the first six weeks, the group getting placebo actually improved slightly faster than the group getting creatine. But when those groups switched between getting placebo and creatine, that (formerly placebo, now creatine) group improved even faster. Just staring at the graph, this suggests some benefit. On Raven’s matrices, the same thing happened, but with a greatly reduced magnitude.

They fit a statistical model and report an effect size of 0.17 standard deviations for backwards digit span (~2.5 IQ points, not quite statistically significant) and 0.09 standard deviations for Raven’s matrices (~1 IQ point, not even close to significant). They found no extra benefit for vegetarians, not even a non-significant benefit.

As far as I can tell, this discrepancy has never been convincingly explained. Rae et al.’s 2003 experiment seems well done. The results are too large to be explained by p-hacking and too statistically significant to be explained by random noise. Maybe for some reason, Rae et al.’s cohort had lower baseline creatine levels? It’s very odd. But history suggests that when an exciting result is followed by a disappointing replication, we should bet on the disappointing replication.
What about all the other RCTs? Doesn’t this call for a meta-analysis?

In principle, yes. The trouble is, most of the studies don’t report the numbers needed for a good meta-analysis. They do some experiment giving creatine to half of people and placebo to the other half, and measure how those groups do on some cognitive test. Then they fit some statistical model and report p-values or whatever. But they never actually publish the raw means and standard deviations.16
Fortunately for us, Xu et al. (2024) contacted the authors for all those trials and got their raw data. According to their meta-analysis, creatine had the following effects.

Unfortunately for us, that paper is bad. They claim that several of these results are statistically significant, but a 2026 commentary points out that they made an error that amounts to double-counting the same data for several studies.17 For that reason, I haven’t shown their (incorrect) confidence intervals. If computed correctly, I suspect none of the results would be statistically significant. Technically, the above point estimates are also wrong, although the error shouldn’t systematically bias them in either direction.

In general, I have to tell you that I really don’t trust this paper. It’s very sloppy with tons of missing details. But as far as I can tell, no one else has ever assembled the data needed to do a good meta-analysis. So I think those numbers are the best summary we have.
So who can we trust?

I’ll tell you who I trust: The European Food and Safety Authority (EFSA). In 2024, a firm selling creatine applied to the EU to be allowed to advertise cognitive benefits. This led the EFSA to publish Creatine and improvement in cognitive function: Evaluation of a health claim pursuant to article 13(5) of regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.
Here’s what they have to say (I’ve cut references for readability):

The Panel considers that, overall, the 10 human intervention studies […] do not show a consistent effect of creatine supplementation on cognitive function. The Panel notes that the acute effect of creatine on working memory reported in some studies […] was not observed at lower creatine doses […] or with continuous consumption of creatine. The Panel also notes that the effect of creatine […] reported in one study is an isolated finding across the body of evidence, where no effect of creatine supplementation was observed on other cognitive domains, including different facets of memory (episodic, short‐term, visual), verbal fluency, attention, alertness, processing speed, psychomotor speed, executive function and general cognitive ability/flexibility and fluid intelligence. Finally, the Panel notes that the three intervention studies conducted in diseased individuals do not support an effect of creatine supplementation on cognition.

I think we should consider this definitive. I’d go so far as to say this document probably represents the greatest effort our civilization has ever made to understand if creatine has cognitive benefits.

But we need to remember the ESFA’s role. They’re asking if creatine has been proven to have cognitive benefits, because they’re deciding if it should be legal to advertise cognitive benefits. They say no and I believe them. But that doesn’t mean there are no cognitive benefits.
Are there other reviews of the RCTs?
Yes. Here are all the recent reviews I could find, with a few representative quotes from each:
“Performance on cognitive tasks stayed unchanged in young individuals.”
“Vegetarians responded better than meat-eaters in memory tasks”
“may improve the performance in some cognitive tasks, particularly in stressful conditions (e.g. mental fatigue, exhaustive exercise).”
“supplementation studies concomitantly assessing brain creatine levels and cognitive function are needed”
“Vegans do not intake sufficient […] creatine to ensure the levels necessary for maintaining optimal cognitive output.”
“Closer examination of [the evidence] suggests that there may be more positive outcomes of supplementation than the research so far provides.”

On average, the RCTs do find a small positive effect, just not a statistically significant positive effect. As I so often point out, that’s exactly what we would expect if the true effect were positive but small. But it’s also entirely possible that this is due to random chance or p-hacking or publication bias. Gwern contacted one author and found that publication bias did in fact occur.

Overall, I think the RCTs provide very weak evidence in favor of a small benefit for healthy adults. (Perhaps 0.1 to 0.3 standard deviations, depending on the measure.) I also think they provide moderate evidence against a larger effect for healthy adults (above, say, 0.5 standard deviations) and weak evidence for a small benefit for adults that are “stressed” in some way that might diminish creatine, such as being older, vegan, or physically exhausted.
Can you summarize the evidence in favor of creatine making you smarter?
I would love to do that:
Creatine is special. Very few nutrients really make you stronger, but creatine does.
Few parts of the body other than muscles use significant creatine, but the brain does.
Creatine can cross the blood-brain barrier.
Creatine is vital for the brain to function correctly.
Supplementing creatine probably increases creatine levels in the brain, at least a little.
Some RCTs suggest a cognitive benefit.
Can you summarize the evidence against creatine making you smarter?
Yes:
We don’t fully understand how the brain uses creatine. There is no clear mechanistic story for why supplementing creatine should make you smarter.
The best analogy for how the brain uses creatine is how your muscles use creatine for endurance exercise. But creatine has little benefit for endurance exercise.
It hasn’t been firmly established how much (or if) supplementing creatine increases creatine levels in the brain.
The RCTs suggest a benefit that is quite small, on the order of 1 to 3 IQ points.
The RCTs are not statistically significant.
Does creatine make you smarter?
I don’t know. Maybe a little.

You could make an argument like this: Creatine is crucial for the brain (somehow) so it’s safest to keep levels high, just in case. But I’m not sure I buy that. Creatine is crucial for the brain but there are several hints that evolution knows that, and so regulates levels in the brain more tightly than in muscles.

I might buy that argument for vegetarians or vegans. But there is scant experimental evidence for extra cognitive benefits in those groups, and even some evidence that vegetarians may not have much lower brain creatine levels, despite vastly lower consumption.

And if creatine is helpful, the likely benefit is probably quite small. Say you think there’s a 50% chance creatine increases IQ by 1 point and a 50% chance it’s useless. Is it actually worth the trouble of taking 5 grams of creatine every day for an expected increase of 0.5 IQ points? I’m not sure.
Technically, they found an increase in dihydrotestosterone (DHT) but not testosterone. ↩

Conveniently, in typical cellular conditions, the body can extract around 100 J of energy from 1 gram of ATP. So we can convert 1 gram ≈ 100 J and 1 gram per second ≈ 100 J / second. You may recall from high school that a watt is defined as 1 watt = Joule per second. ↩

Wikipedia quotes a paper saying people make / recycle around 50 kilograms per day. That would imply that people make around 0.5787 grams per second. But this is in tension with the idea that people use 100 watts at rest. Since that 100 watt number seems to be more strongly established, I think 1 gram per second is a better estimate. ↩

Why do you breathe? You breathe because your mitochondria need oxygen to make ATP. When you exercise, you breathe faster so that your mitochondria can make more ATP. You can actually calculate how much ATP your mitochondria make using your VO₂ max score: For each liter of oxygen you use, you make ~21,000 joules of energy, corresponding to ~210 grams of ATP. If you have a typical VO₂ max score of 40 mL/kg/min and you weigh 70 kg, that means you are using 2.8 liters of oxygen per minute, which corresponds to ~588 grams of ATP per minute or ~9.8 grams per second. ↩

A Tour de France cyclist might burn 1500 or even 2000 watts for hours, meaning they are producing ~20 grams of ATP. They can do this because they’ve trained their bodies to have more mitochondria and better oxygen delivery to those mitochondria. But it takes a few seconds for the body to ramp up and start producing this much power. ↩
The “T” in “ATP” is for “triple”, meaning there are three phosphate groups. The “D” is for “di”, meaning there are two phosphate groups. ↩

There’s also stored energy in the form of glycogen. This takes a few seconds to come online, and lasts a few minutes. In a sprint, you aren’t limited by glycogen stores running out, but by having too much acid buildup.

        The chemical energy stored in (phosph)ocreatine molecules. (Recharges ATP)

translations: 肌酸是一种类似类固醇的奇怪激素或药物吗？
不是。肌酸是一种营养物质。大多数杂食者每天从肉类中摄入一两克肌酸。你的身体每天也会合成一两克。你需要肌酸来在细胞内传递能量。它是正常且并不奇怪的。
肌酸会增加睾酮水平吗？
不太可能。这种担忧源于2009年一项针对16名男性橄榄球运动员的研究。1 但该研究被认为极其可疑。至少有另外十二项研究发现没有变化，或者变化在生理上微不足道。除此之外，肌酸会增加睾酮的说法也站不住脚，因为我们知道肌酸的作用机制，它与激素毫无关系。
肌酸会让你脱发吗？
不会。或者说：
从来没有研究报道过这一点。
有一项研究甚至得出了相反的结论。
从机制上讲，没有理由认为会发生这种情况。
相反，有充分的机制理由认为这不会发生。
这些谣言都可以追溯到基于那同一项2009年研究的推测。但该研究已被后来的研究反驳，而且无论如何它并没有测量头发。一切皆有可能，但据我所知，肌酸促进头发生长的说法同样说得通。如果你真的对此感到担忧：你打算不吃肉了吗？
肌酸安全吗？
可能是安全的。国际运动营养学会表示：
现有的针对健康人群和患病人群（从婴儿到老年人）的短期和长期研究表明，在长达5年的时间里，每天摄入0.3至0.8克/公斤的剂量，始终表明补充肌酸不会对健康造成不良风险，并可能提供多种健康和运动表现方面的益处。
它已被广泛研究，未发现任何风险。它的作用机制也没有暗示任何风险。每天补充几克并不会让你远远超出人们从正常食物中获取的范围。
肌酸能让你变得更强壮吗？
是的。一种补充剂能有如此强大且一致的证据是非常罕见的。一篇被广泛引用的综述指出，短期补充可使最大力量/强度提高5-15%。这反过来可能会增加力量训练带来的长期收益。肌酸还能将冲刺表现提高1-5%。不过，对于长跑等耐力运动，似乎没有什么益处，即使有也很少。
但肌酸是如何让你变得更强壮的呢？
在回答这个问题之前，我能先讲讲肌肉是如何运作的吗？
……可以吗？
太好了！肌肉是这样运作的：
所有细胞内部都漂浮着一种叫做 ATP 的分子，细胞用它来提供能量。
肌肉细胞内含有一种叫做肌球蛋白的蛋白质。
当 ATP 撞上肌球蛋白时，肌球蛋白会将 ATP 分解为 ADP。这会释放能量，并被肌球蛋白以弹性应变的形式物理捕获。
当受到神经元触发时，肌球蛋白会释放这种机械能。
当你决定移动手臂时，你的大脑会触发许多肌肉细胞，精心协调肌球蛋白的抽动，从而形成大规模的运动。
现在，有一点对我们的故事至关重要：以 ATP 形式储存的能量非常少。你的身体含有约100克 ATP，代表约10,000焦耳的能量。2 但你的身体在静息状态下会消耗约100瓦的功率。因此，你储存的 ATP 仅够维持你存活约100秒。如果你冲刺，你很容易消耗约3000瓦的功率，这将在约3秒内耗尽你所有储存的 ATP。
通过进食的魔力，你总是在不断制造更多的 ATP。通常情况下，你的线粒体每秒能将约 1 克 ADP 循环转化为 ATP，这正是维持你生命所需的量。3 如果你开始跑步，你的身体可以通过加快呼吸和心跳等技巧，将这一速度提升至每秒约 10 克。4 但线粒体需要一两分钟才能真正全速运转起来。5
那么，为什么我能冲刺超过三秒钟呢？
因为肌酸充当了与 ATP 储备相耦合的额外能量储备。在你摄入或合成肌酸后，60% 会转化为磷酸肌酸。这是由一种酶完成的，它抓住一个肌酸分子和一个 ATP 分子，并在它们之间转移一个磷酸基团。这会将肌酸“充电”成磷酸肌酸，并将 ATP“放电”成 ADP。6
但如果你的 ATP 水平下降——例如因为你正在躲避老虎——那些酶就会反向运行，这意味着它们将磷酸肌酸“放电”成肌酸，并将 ADP 重新“充电”成 ATP。这几乎是瞬间发生的，因此 ATP 和磷酸肌酸会以相同的速率消耗。7
在休息状态下，你肌肉中的磷酸肌酸含量大约是 ATP 的 3 到 4 倍。因此，磷酸肌酸中的“额外”能量储备远大于 ATP 本身的“基础”储备。这就是为什么你能冲刺十秒钟，而不仅仅是三秒钟。
补充肌酸会增加肌肉细胞中的肌酸水平吗？
是的。典型水平如下：
素食者：100 mmol / kg
杂食者：120 mmol / kg
补充肌酸的人：140 mmol / kg
所以，一切似乎都说得通了。如果你补充肌酸，你的肌酸水平会增加约 16.67%，这意味着短期总能量储备增加了约 12.5%。8 这与肌酸试验中观察到的 5-15% 的力量增长相符。9 肌酸试验发现它对耐力运动几乎没有益处，这也说得通。如果你没有突然的爆发性活动，更大的短期能量储备对你并没有真正的帮助。
但这难道不奇怪吗？
嗯，我觉得这很奇怪。在其他条件相同的情况下，力量越大越好。身体已经知道如何制造肌酸。如果你能仅仅通过提高肌酸水平就获得更多力量且没有任何缺点，那么进化难道不应该早就这么做了吗？某种版本的阿尔吉侬论点会认为，肌酸如此有效这一事实本应是不可能的。
你可能会认为较高的肌酸水平在某种程度上是有害的，这就是为什么进化没有让它们变得更高。但这似乎是错误的。肌酸水平会根据你的饮食自然变化。如果较高水平是有害的，进化本可以将其降低。但它并没有。它只是任由其变化。
通常，进化会让我们变得“更差”以减少能量消耗，因为进化讨厌我们饿死。10 但身体每天只消耗 1-2 卡路里来合成肌酸，而且肌肉细胞中更多的肌酸并没有任何显著的代谢成本。
我认为无聊的解释是，对于我们进化的祖先来说，短期力量的适度增加并不是什么大不了的事。我们是耐力型狩猎者，而不是极限单次硬拉狩猎者。11 此外，更多的肌酸会导致你的肌肉细胞吸收一些额外的水分，这会略微增加长跑时的能量消耗。12 所以，如果你碰巧从肉类中获得了额外的肌酸，那很好。如果没有，也无所谓。在肌酸随饮食波动的范围内，我怀疑肌酸水平对繁殖成功率并没有太大影响。
尽管如此，我们必须承认肌酸是很不寻常的。我希望我们能告诉自己的身体：“嘿，我们有取之不尽的食物。别再担心节约能量了，集中精力变得更强吧。”但我们能做到这一点的方法寥寥无几。据我所知，已被证明能增强力量的常规营养素清单只有：蛋白质、肌酸、β-丙氨酸，仅此而已。
所以肌酸很特别。而且肌酸能让你变得更强壮一点。它也能让你变得更聪明一点吗？
大脑会使用肌酸吗？
是的。身体的大部分部位并不含有大量的肌酸。但大脑含有，肌肉、心脏和睾丸也是如此。神经元利用它来玩和肌肉一样的游戏，即与 ATP 和磷酸基团等相互作用。
大脑中有多少肌酸？
可能是肌肉中的一半。这里我们关注的数值是磷酸肌酸与 ATP 的比例，它表明磷酸肌酸能在多大程度上增加局部能量储备。我们在上面看到，在肌肉中，这个比例是 3 到 4。在大脑中，数据有些模糊，但比例似乎更接近 1.5 到 2.13。
但这是为什么呢？为什么大脑会使用肌酸？
好问题！大脑不像肌肉那样有爆发性的能量消耗。是的，尽管大脑只占体重的 2% 左右，却消耗了约 20% 的卡路里。但大脑的特别之处在于，它需要所有这些能量仅仅是为了维持基本运转，而且不会随着使用量的增加而显著上升。与普遍的误解相反，苦思冥想并不会燃烧明显更多的卡路里。（演示：开始苦思冥想，看着你的心率并不会增加。）
所以肌肉在冲刺时使用肌酸。但大脑没有冲刺。那么大脑到底用肌酸来做什么？
最常见的理论似乎是这样的：实际上，肌肉不仅将肌酸作为额外的能量储备库。它们还利用它在细胞内传递能量。你看，肌酸在细胞内的扩散速度比 ATP 快。因此，即使在耐力运动中，肌酸仍在被使用：线粒体附近的酶利用 ATP 将肌酸“充能”为磷酸肌酸，而肌球蛋白附近的酶则利用这种磷酸肌酸将 ADP 重新“充能”为 ATP。尽管肌酸的净变化为零，但它有助于将能量从线粒体“穿梭”到肌球蛋白。
根据这个理论，神经元和肌肉细胞的共同点在于，当它们被触发时，细胞的某些局部会消耗大量能量。因此，即使你的大脑不“冲刺”，它仍然会使用肌酸来避免局部能量赤字。
还有实验证据表明肌酸对大脑很重要。我们培育出了经过基因改造的小鼠，它们的大脑缺乏在肌酸和磷酸肌酸之间相互转化所需的酶。它们表现出严重受限的空间学习能力，并且大脑也略小。
有些人也会自然患有肌酸缺乏症。在某些变异中，人们难以合成肌酸。这会导致全身肌酸水平降低，包括 95% 肌酸所在的骨骼肌。然而，主要症状与大脑有关，即智力障碍。肌肉无力和癫痫发作也很常见。另一些人患有肌酸转运蛋白缺乏症，这意味着肌酸无法穿过血脑屏障。这仅导致大脑中肌酸水平降低。这同样会导致智力障碍，并且通常伴有肌肉无力或癫痫发作。（尽管肌肉细胞本身具有正常的肌酸水平，但仍会出现这种肌肉无力。）14
不知何故，肌酸对大脑非常重要。
补充肌酸会增加大脑中的肌酸水平吗？
可能会，尽管可能不如在肌肉中增加得多。
肌酸确实可以穿过血脑屏障。然而，帮助其穿过的蛋白质并不丰富，而且有迹象表明，长期摄入肌酸会导致该蛋白质表达下调。大脑本身也能合成一些肌酸，这同样可能因长期摄入而受到下调。
当然，你可以直接给人们补充肌酸，看看他们的大脑会发生什么变化。大约有十几项这样的研究。大多数研究报告称增加了3%到10%，尽管也有少数报告称没有变化。然而，由于大脑难以直接接触，这些研究依赖于磁共振波谱技术，而且有人认为这些测量结果并不可靠。
对于无法合成肌酸的人来说，口服补充似乎能使大脑中的肌酸水平恢复正常。（通常会残留一些认知障碍。有一名患者在三周大时被确诊并开始补充肌酸，没有出现智力障碍。）因此，在某些情况下，补充肌酸确实可以增加大脑中的肌酸水平。
我最好的猜测是，补充肌酸通常确实会增加大脑中的肌酸水平，增加3%到10%是合理的。但证据并不是特别充分。
为什么人们会对肌酸具有认知益处产生兴趣？
因为 Rae et al. (2003) 的研究。他们在澳大利亚选取了45名健康的素食或纯素食大学生。他们进行了一项交叉试验，其中一半人每天摄入5克肌酸，持续六周，随后是六周的洗脱期，然后另一半人摄入肌酸。他们的结果令人惊叹，在瑞文推理测验（RAPM）和倒背数字广度（BDS）上都有巨大的提升：
在他们的分析中，肌酸使 BDS 提高了1.19个标准差，使 RAPM 提高了1.76个标准差。如果我们将这些数字转换为智商分数（其中1个标准差对应15个智商点），那就意味着分别提高了17.85和26.4个智商点。在这两项测试中，结果都具有高度显著性（p < 0.0001）。
这能复现吗？

不能。在那篇论文发表后，各个研究团队尝试了类似的实验，但没有人发现如此大或具有统计学意义的效果。经过二十年悬而未决的结果，Sandkühler et al. (2023) 决定进行一次决定性的复现。在我看来，这是关于肌酸认知益处方面质量最高的 RCT。他们很大程度上借鉴了 Rae et al. 的实验设计，尽管他们在德国进行了实验，使用了更大的123人样本，其中一半是非素食者，并且他们取消了洗脱期。以下是他们的主要结果：
（T1 显示基线时的测试结果。T2 显示服用肌酸或安慰剂六周后的结果。T3 显示又过六周后的结果，此时安慰剂组交叉换成了肌酸，反之亦然。）
总体而言，随着时间的推移，每个人的表现都变好了，这可能是由于练习效应。在倒背数字广度测试中，在最初的六周里，服用安慰剂的组实际上比服用肌酸的组进步得稍快一些。但是当这些组在服用安慰剂和肌酸之间进行切换时，那个（原先服用安慰剂，现在服用肌酸的）组进步得更快了。仅从图表来看，这表明存在一些益处。在瑞文推理测验中，也发生了同样的情况，但幅度大大减小了。
他们拟合了一个统计模型，报告称倒背数字广度的效应量为0.17个标准差（约2.5个IQ点，不太具有统计学意义），瑞文推理测验的效应量为0.09个标准差（约1个IQ点，远未达到显著水平）。他们发现这对素食主义者没有额外益处，甚至连不显著的益处都没有。
据我所知，这种差异从未得到过令人信服的解释。Rae 等人 2003 年的实验似乎做得很严谨。其结果效应太大，无法用 p-hacking 来解释；统计学意义太强，也无法用随机噪声来解释。也许出于某种原因，Rae 等人的队列基线肌酸水平较低？这非常奇怪。但历史经验表明，当一个令人兴奋的结果随后迎来了令人失望的重复实验时，我们应该把赌注押在令人失望的重复实验上。
那么其他所有的随机对照试验（RCT）呢？这难道不需要进行一项荟萃分析吗？
原则上是的。问题在于，大多数研究并没有报告进行高质量荟萃分析所需的数据。他们进行某种实验，给一半人服用肌酸，另一半人服用安慰剂，并测量这些组在某些认知测试中的表现。然后他们拟合某种统计模型并报告 p 值等指标。但他们从未真正发表原始的均值和标准差。16
幸运的是，Xu 等人（2024）联系了所有这些试验的作者并获取了原始数据。根据他们的荟萃分析，肌酸具有以下效果。
不幸的是，那篇论文质量很差。他们声称其中几项结果具有统计学意义，但 2026 年的一篇评论指出，他们犯了一个错误，相当于在几项研究中对相同数据进行了重复计算。17 出于这个原因，我没有展示他们（错误的）置信区间。如果计算正确，我怀疑所有结果都不会具有统计学意义。严格来说，上述的点估计也是错误的，尽管该误差不应在任何方向上造成系统性偏差。
总的来说，我必须告诉你，我真的不信任这篇论文。它非常草率，遗漏了大量细节。但据我所知，没有其他人曾收集过进行高质量荟萃分析所需的数据。因此，我认为这些数字是我们目前能得到的最好总结。
那么我们还能信任谁呢？
我来告诉你我信任谁：欧洲食品安全局（EFSA）。2024 年，一家销售肌酸的公司向欧盟申请，要求允许其宣传肌酸的认知益处。这促使 EFSA 发布了《肌酸与认知功能改善：根据第 1924/2006 号法规（EC）第 13(5) 条对健康声称的评估》。
以下是他们的说法（为了便于阅读，我删去了参考文献）：

专家组认为，总体而言，10项人类干预研究[…]并未显示补充肌酸对认知功能有一致的影响。专家组指出，一些研究[…]中报告的肌酸对工作记忆的急性作用，在较低肌酸剂量[…]或持续摄入肌酸的情况下并未观察到。专家组还指出，一项研究报告的肌酸[…]作用是整个证据体系中的一个孤立发现，在其他认知领域均未观察到补充肌酸的作用，包括记忆的不同方面（情景记忆、短期记忆、视觉记忆）、言语流畅性、注意力、警觉性、处理速度、精神运动速度、执行功能以及一般认知能力/灵活性和流体智力。最后，专家组指出，在患病个体中进行的3项干预研究并不支持补充肌酸对认知有影响。
我认为我们应该将其视为定论。我甚至敢说，这份文件可能代表了我们人类文明为了解肌酸是否具有认知益处而做出的最大努力。
但我们需要记住 EFSA 的角色。他们是在问肌酸是否已被证明具有认知益处，因为他们正在决定是否应该允许宣传其认知益处。他们说没有，我相信他们。但这并不意味着它没有认知益处。
还有其他关于随机对照试验（RCTs）的综述吗？
有。以下是我能找到的所有近期综述，并附有每篇综述的几句代表性引文：
“年轻人在认知任务上的表现保持不变。”
“素食者在记忆任务中的表现优于肉食者”
“可能会改善某些认知任务的表现，特别是在压力条件下（例如精神疲劳、力竭运动）。”
“需要同时评估大脑肌酸水平和认知功能的补充研究”
“纯素食者摄入的肌酸不足[…]，无法确保维持最佳认知输出所需的水平。”
“对[证据]的仔细审查表明，补充肌酸可能比目前研究所显示的带来更多积极结果。”
平均而言，随机对照试验确实发现了一个微小的正面效应，只是没有达到统计学上的显著正面效应。正如我经常指出的那样，如果真实效应是正面的但很小，这正是我们会预期到的结果。但这也有可能完全是由于随机概率、p-hacking 或发表偏倚造成的。Gwern 联系了一位作者，发现确实发生了发表偏倚。
总体而言，我认为随机对照试验提供了非常微弱的证据，支持其对健康成年人有轻微益处。（根据测量指标的不同，可能在0.1到0.3个标准差之间。）我还认为，它们提供了中等强度的证据，反对其对健康成年人有较大影响（比如超过0.5个标准差），并提供了微弱的证据，支持其对以某种可能消耗肌酸的方式处于“压力”下的成年人有轻微益处，例如老年人、纯素食者或体力透支者。
你能总结一下支持肌酸能让人变聪明的证据吗？
我很乐意这么做：
肌酸很特别。很少有营养素能真正让你变得更强壮，但肌酸可以。
除了肌肉外，身体很少有其他部位会大量消耗肌酸，但大脑会。
肌酸可以穿过血脑屏障。
肌酸对大脑正常运作至关重要。
补充肌酸可能会增加大脑中的肌酸水平，至少会有一点增加。
一些随机对照试验（RCTs）表明存在认知方面的益处。
你能总结一下反对肌酸能让人变聪明的证据吗？
可以：
我们尚未完全了解大脑是如何使用肌酸的。对于为什么补充肌酸能让人变聪明，目前还没有明确的机制解释。
关于大脑如何使用肌酸，最好的类比是肌肉如何在耐力运动中使用肌酸。但肌酸对耐力运动几乎没有益处。
补充肌酸能在多大程度上（或是否能够）提高大脑中的肌酸水平，目前尚未得到确凿证实。
随机对照试验显示的益处非常小，大约在1到3个IQ点（智商点）的量级。
这些随机对照试验在统计学上并不显著。
肌酸能让你变聪明吗？
我不知道。也许有一点吧。
你可以提出这样的论点：肌酸对大脑至关重要（以某种方式），所以为了以防万一，保持高水平是最安全的。但我不确定我是否认同这一点。肌酸对大脑确实至关重要，但有几点迹象表明，进化过程知道这一点，因此对大脑中肌酸水平的调节比对肌肉的调节更为严格。
对于素食主义者或纯素食者，我可能会接受这个论点。但是，关于这些群体具有额外认知益处的实验证据非常少，甚至有证据表明，尽管摄入量大幅降低，素食者大脑中的肌酸水平可能并没有低多少。
而且，如果肌酸确实有帮助，可能的益处大概也非常小。假设你认为肌酸有50%的几率使IQ提高1分，有50%的几率毫无用处。为了预期增加0.5个IQ点，每天服用5克肌酸真的值得费这个事吗？我不确定。
严格来说，他们发现双氢睾酮（DHT）有所增加，但睾酮并未增加。 ↩
方便的是，在典型的细胞条件下，人体可以从1克ATP中提取约100焦耳的能量。因此我们可以换算为1克 ≈ 100焦耳，以及1克/秒 ≈ 100焦耳/秒。你可能还记得高中时学过，瓦特的定义是1瓦特 = 焦耳/秒。 ↩
维基百科引用了一篇论文，指出人体每天产生/回收约50公斤的ATP。这意味着人体每秒产生约0.5787克ATP。但这与人体在静息状态下消耗100瓦特能量的观点相矛盾。由于100瓦特这个数字似乎更为确凿，我认为每秒1克是一个更好的估算值。 ↩

你为什么会呼吸？你呼吸是因为你的线粒体需要氧气来制造ATP。当你运动时，你会呼吸得更快，以便你的线粒体能够制造更多的ATP。你实际上可以使用你的最大摄氧量（VO₂ max）得分来计算你的线粒体制造了多少ATP：你每消耗一升氧气，就会产生约21,000焦耳的能量，相当于约210克ATP。如果你有一个典型的40 mL/kg/min的VO₂ max得分，且体重为70公斤，这意味着你每分钟消耗2.8升氧气，相当于每分钟约588克ATP，或每秒约9.8克ATP。 ↩
环法自行车赛的选手可能会连续数小时消耗1500甚至2000瓦特的能量，这意味着他们每秒产生约20克ATP。他们能做到这一点，是因为他们通过训练使身体拥有了更多的线粒体，并能向这些线粒体更好地输送氧气。但身体需要几秒钟的时间来加速并开始产生这么大的功率。 ↩
“ATP”中的“T”代表“三”（triple），意味着有三个磷酸基团。“D”代表“二”（di），意味着有两个磷酸基团。 ↩

还有以糖原形式储存的能量。这需要几秒钟才能被激活，并持续几分钟。在短跑中，你的限制因素不是糖原储备耗尽，而是酸积累过多。因此，实际上，人体有五个级别的缓存能量：储存在肌球蛋白弹性应变中的机械能。储存在 ATP 分子中的化学能。（为肌球蛋白充能）储存在（磷酸）肌酸分子中的化学能。（为 ATP 充能）储存在糖原中的化学能。（为 ATP 充能，从而为肌酸充能）储存在食物和脂肪中的化学能。（用于为糖原（食物）和 ATP（食物或脂肪）充能，从而为肌酸充能。）↩
之所以是 12.5% 而不是 16.67%，是因为你的短期能量储备约 75% 是磷酸肌酸，约 25% 是 ATP，而补充肌酸并不会增加 ATP。↩
我不确定这种数学计算在多大程度上真正解释了为什么我们在肌酸研究中看到力量增加了 5-15%，还是说这仅仅是个巧合。这是从“短期能量储备增加 X%”到“最大卧推增加 X%”的跨越。↩
与我们的进化祖先相比，我们有着漫长而无助的童年、较低的肌肉量和更小的大脑。↩
考虑到在非国家社会中有多少人死于暴力，我确实对此感到好奇。但是，多出 10% 的力量能有多频繁地改变结果呢？↩
我觉得很有趣，许多资料将额外的水分滞留称为“常见副作用”甚至报告统计数据，而据我所知，这基本上是由物理学规律决定的必然结果。↩
Tsuji 等人报告称灰质中的磷酸肌酸与 ATP 比率为 0.77，白质中为 2.18；Lu 等人报告称整个大脑中约为 1.45；而 Hetherington 等人报告称白质中为 1.0，灰质中为 1.6，小脑中为 2.1。↩
合成肌酸困难可以通过补充肌酸来治疗。肌酸转运蛋白缺陷目前尚无有效的治疗方法。↩
写下这句话后，我后来注意到这项实验显然是由有效利他主义基金会、Effective Ventures 以及（著名的 AI 对齐研究员）Paul Christiano 个人资助的。↩
我知道这听起来很奇怪，但这非常普遍。每个人都想确立真理，而不仅仅是创造数据让别人去确立真理。考虑到他们的激励机制，很难责怪他们。↩
Prokopidis 等人在 2022 年的另一项荟萃分析中发现了类似的结果，但显然也存在类似的问题。Prokopidis 等人值得称赞，因为他们承认了这个问题并发布了更正。然而，Prokopidis 等人只关注记忆力，而且他们似乎是在使用同一批人的前后得分进行对比，而不是在安慰剂组和肌酸组之间进行比较。↩

Trump's America can't even win a rigged game (permalink)
Here's a sentence that stopped me in my tracks last week: "The statement that 'the cemeteries are full of indispensable people' is just as true of nations, and in particular the US":
https://crookedtimber.org/2026/07/16/55382/

The writer is John Quiggin, writing about the fact that, under Trump, the world has raced through a series of seismic shifts in how it organizes itself, rushing to fill an America-shaped void in its dealings.

This is a subject that's very much on my mind. As November Kelly says, Trump inherited a poker game rigged in his favor and then flipped the table over because he resented having to pretend to play at all. The "international rules-based order" that gave America oversight and control over the world's militaries, finances, trade, and communications was always a better deal for America than it was for the rest of the world.

The long persistence of this system doesn't mean that other countries liked it. The reason the American century endured for as long as it did was that the toll that America extracted from the world was always lower than the cost of making a new system. Just as people stay on Facebook because they love their friends more than they hate Mark Zuckerberg, the nations of the world let America control their systems because they feared the cost and difficulty of building a new system more than they resented letting America dictate and tax every part of their politics and economies.

That's where Trump comes in. The price of doing business with Trump is, effectively, infinity. If you buck Trump, he doubles down and demands twice as much. If you capitulate to Trump, he interprets it as weakness and comes back for three times as much. There are no deals to be made with Trump, only temporary measures that last until his next Fox and Friends binge or chance encounter with a ridiculous conspiracy theory.

Take Canada: in 2018, Trump tore up NAFTA – the deal that Bush Sr and Clinton crammed down Mexico and Canada's throats – and replaced it with USMCA, a trade treaty that was even more advantageous to America. Then, within months of his 2024 election, Trump tore up USMCA and replaced it with a chaotic series of tariffs that swung around wildly from 25% to 100% to (as of this week) 50%:
https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/07/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-imposes-additional-tariffs-on-canada/

Trump has no coherent reason for this new tariff. Canada has bent over backwards to give Trump everything he wants and more. Despite some high-minded words at Davos about the need for "middle powers" to decouple from the USA, PM Mark Carney has given Trump everything he could ask for. Carney allowed Palantir – a company that makes no bones about being an agent of Trump's will – inside the most sensitive parts of the Canadian military. Carney dropped his plan to charge US tech companies a 3% tax. Carney is firing tens of thousands of civil servants and replacing them with chatbots, the majority of which will be operated by US companies, running on US servers.

Sure, Canada's imposed some retaliatory tariffs on US products, but that's just a way of making everything Canadians buy more expensive, which is a weird way of punishing America. It's like punching yourself in the face as hard as you can in the hopes that the downstairs neighbour says "ouch." Meanwhile, Carney has consistently ignored US interference in Canadian politics, including the tsunami of dark money pouring into the Alberta separatist movement – a bid by Trump to literally steal an entire province.

Give Trump everything he asks for and he'll demand more. Deny Trump anything and he'll demand more. Sign a contract with Trump and he'll break it. Send Trump an invoice and he'll stiff you. For Trump, "the art of the deal" can be summed up in one word: renege.
This is why – as David Dayen writes – there will likely be no peace deal in Iran for so long as Trump is in office. Why would the Iranians sign any deal with Trump when they know Trump will break it?
https://prospect.org/2026/07/10/aftermath-wars-on/

Last Christmas, I gave a speech in Hamburg about "the post-American internet" that the rest of the world has the chance to build now that Trump has zeroed-out all the value it used to get from playing by America's tech policy rules, even as Trump has weaponized US tech companies to attack world officials who buck his agenda:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

After that speech, I wrote a book (The Post-American Internet) that Farrar, Straus and Giroux will publish in August 2027. In the book, I describe the role that "trusted third parties" (T3P) play in complex transactions. Think of an escrow agent who holds onto the deed for the house you're buying from the seller until you hand over the money, and then forwards the deed to you and the money to the seller.

The more complex a transaction is, the more it needs a T3P. For most of the past century, the US has been the world's T3P. Most of the world's transoceanic fiber optic lines make landfall in the US and interconnect to one another in US data centres. Most of the world's international transactions are conducted in dollars and are cleared through US-controlled platforms like SWIFT. Through its aid programs, the US sets the health and public services agenda for billions of non-Americans, and the US has military installations in more than 100 countries. The US trains the world's militaries, it supplies (and withholds) information from the world's intelligence agencies, and it runs the IT infrastructure powering the world's government agencies and critical infrastructure, from tractors to medical equipment.

Right from the start, the US was never an entirely trustworthy "trusted third party." There were plenty of moments where the US abused its control over its "neutral" platforms to serve the American national interest at the expense of the countries that relied on those platforms.

But those violations were either covert or carried out under some kind of legal rubric ("the rules-based international order"). You'd probably continue to trust an escrow agent that obeyed court orders to hold onto the money after handing over the deed. That trust might persist even if the escrow agent withheld the money on the say-so of a DA or sheriff, even without a court order. You might even continue to trust the escrow agent if they sometimes said, "I'm going to hang onto this money for 72 hours because I think there might be something weird in this deal."

Same goes for the escrow agent who has a secret side-hustle with the local land-registry office and realtors that lets them skim a few points off every deal and scoop up the best properties through a shell company. Provided you never find out about this, you'll happily hire that escrow agent to handle your property deal.

Trump is the escrow agent who keeps the money and the deed, then announces he did it because the seller was a fentanyl dealer and the buyer was a lizard-person; and then publishes a long screed on Truth Social calling everyone who criticises him a terrorist, promising to do it again next time.

Even if you need to sell your house, and even if Trump is the only escrow agent you can find, you're just not going to trust him with your deed or the money. As GW Bush says, "Fool me once, shame on…shame on you. Fool me – you can't get fooled again."

Back to Quiggin: the US was the world's indispensable nation, and the cemeteries of history are full of indispensable nations. As Quiggin writes, Europe and Ukraine have largely given up on US military protection from Russia and are building their own capacity, already surpassing the US in drone and artillery capabilities. The US can no longer credibly provide missiles and anti-missile defenses, not after Trump used up America's stockpiles in his pointless, endless war in Iran.

Quiggin notes that the consensus case against the EU as a military power held that Europe "lacks the capacity to project power globally" and that it is "too disunited to act effectively." Per Quiggin, these only matter if you believe that the post-American military order will look and act like the American system that Trump just trashed. Trump has a chud "Secretary of War" who kidnaps foreign leaders and can't reliably get oil through the Strait of Hormuz – if that's the dividend from "unity" and "projecting power," you can keep it.

On finance, Quiggin notes that the EU is racing to break its reliance on SWIFT, Visa and Mastercard, and the more Trump weaponizes these against institutions like the International Criminal Court, the faster this transition will go.

America's load-bearing private institutions – like the Big Four accounting firms and the bond rating agencies – have self-immolated, thanks to decades of lax regulation by successive US administrations through scandal after scandal. Quiggin points out that there's no reason to replace these giant, structurally important (but terrifyingly unreliable) cartels with trustworthy versions. It's cheaper and more robust to rebuild our economy so that it no longer serves the finance system, returning finance to "its pre-1970s role as a provider of a relatively limited set of services to the real economy."

On manufacturing, Quiggin points to the twin facts of Trump's chaotic tariffs and China's "economic nationalism," which have put the EU in the centre of a new trade order. Here, too, we're getting something new, not a Made-in-Europe version of "the failed globalist dream of the WTO" nor "Trump’s attempts to extort surplus through bilateral bullying":
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/12/opinion/america-trump-nato-europe-world.html

As I said, Quiggin's article has been rattling around in my mind ever since I read it last week, but there's one area where I think Quiggin's got it wrong: the relative difficulty of building a post-American internet.

First, because Quiggin says that the real challenge is building a post-American AI. Sovereign AI is, frankly, nonsense. If Trump turns off all of your country's chatbots, nothing changes. If Trump orders Microsoft to shut off your country's access to Office 365 (as he did to the International Criminal Court and a Brazilian judge who pissed him off), your country would simply cease to function:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/18/their-trillions-our-billions/#eyes-on-the-prize
And if Trump orders John Deere to brick all the tractors in your country, you're gonna starve to death:
https://pluralistic.net/2022/05/08/about-those-kill-switched-ukrainian-tractors/

In the face of these real, non-speculative, immediate, grave threats, focusing on AI – the money-losingest technology in human history, which has consistently underperformed relative to its boosters' promises – is just misguided. If you really want an "AI strategy" for your country, it should be this: wait for the bubble to burst, then buy hardware and talent at fire-sale prices in the wave of ensuing bankruptcies, and use them to extract more performance from free, open source models.

The real digital challenge is building apps and data centres to run everyday administrative, telecoms and e-commerce software on, and then moving your country's, ministries', companies' and households' data over to the new platforms. The hardware and software are challenging, but ultimately straightforward. Raising capital for data centres is just a matter of convincing people to invest in being a kind of landlord, which is among the easier sells to make (and there's plenty of investors who are looking for real alternatives to getting sucked into the AI bubble).

Getting the apps is hard, but there's an army of technologists who are ready for more, after decades of doing fake startups for a Big Tech company to "acqui-hire" and/or toiling to improve ad click-throughs. These people yearn to follow Steve Jobs's injunction to "make a dent in the universe" and they are being chased out of Silicon Valley by ICE chuds who want to send them to Salvadoran slave-labor camps.
There's plenty of talent and capital for the taking.

The real hard part isn't writing or running the code – it's extracting the data, replacing the firmware, and bridging new systems – like post-American social media platforms – into the existing ones. This part is hard because every country in the world has agreed to a trade deal with America wherein they agreed to make it illegal to reverse-engineer US tech exports, in exchange for tariff-free access to US markets. Trump has made the case for abandoning these deals better than I ever could have:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/20/praxis/#acceleration

上周有一句话让我停下脚步：“‘墓地中满是不可或缺的人’这句话对国家而言同样适用，尤其是对美国”：
https://crookedtimber.org/2026/07/16/55382/
作者是 John Quiggin，他写道，在特朗普治下，世界在自我组织方式上经历了一系列剧变，急于填补其交往中出现的美国形状的真空。
这是一个我一直在思考的问题。正如 November Kelly 所说，特朗普继承了一场为他量身操纵的扑克游戏，却因为讨厌必须假装参与而掀翻了桌子。赋予美国对世界军事、金融、贸易和通信的监督与控制权的“基于规则的国际秩序”，对美国而言始终比世界其他国家更划算。
这一体系的长期存在并不意味着其他国家喜欢它。美国世纪之所以能持续这么久，是因为美国从世界汲取的代价始终低于建立新体系的成本。就像人们留在 Facebook 上是因为他们爱朋友胜过恨 Mark Zuckerberg 一样，世界各国让美国控制他们的体系，是因为他们害怕建立新体系的成本和困难，胜过他们讨厌让美国对他们的政治和经济的每个部分发号施令并征税。
这就是特朗普介入的地方。与特朗普做生意的代价实际上是无限的。如果你反抗特朗普，他会变本加厉，要求两倍的东西。如果你向特朗普屈服，他会将其视为软弱，并回来索要三倍的东西。与特朗普没有交易可做，只有持续到他下一次狂看 Fox and Friends 或偶然接触到一个荒谬阴谋论的临时措施。
以加拿大为例：2018年，特朗普撕毁了NAFTA——老布什和克林顿强加给墨西哥和加拿大的协议——并用USMCA取而代之，这是一项对美国更有利的贸易条约。然后，在他2024年当选后的几个月内，特朗普撕毁了USMCA，代之以一系列混乱的关税，这些关税在25%到100%再到（截至本周）50%之间疯狂摇摆：
https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/07/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-imposes-additional-tariffs-on-canada/

特朗普对这项新关税没有站得住脚的理由。加拿大已经竭尽全力满足特朗普的一切要求，甚至有过之而无不及。尽管在达沃斯论坛上有过一些关于“中等强国”需要与美国脱钩的高调言论，但总理马克·卡尼还是满足了特朗普所能要求的一切。卡尼允许 Palantir——一家毫不掩饰自己是特朗普意志代理人身份的公司——进入加拿大军方最敏感的部门。卡尼放弃了对美国科技公司征收3%税收的计划。卡尼正在解雇数万名公务员，并用聊天机器人取代他们，其中大部分机器人将由美国公司运营，运行在美国的服务器上。
当然，加拿大对美国产品征收了一些报复性关税，但这只会让加拿大人购买的所有东西变得更贵，这是一种惩罚美国的奇怪方式。这就像你用尽全力打自己的脸，指望楼下的邻居喊一声“哎哟”。与此同时，卡尼一直无视美国对加拿大政治的干涉，包括涌入阿尔伯塔省分离主义运动的大量黑钱——这是特朗普企图直接窃取整个省份的举动。
满足特朗普的所有要求，他会索要更多。拒绝特朗普的任何要求，他也会索要更多。和特朗普签合同，他会撕毁它。给特朗普寄账单，他会赖账。对特朗普来说，“交易的艺术”可以用一个词来概括：违约。
这就是为什么——正如大卫·达延所写——只要特朗普在任，伊朗就不太可能达成和平协议。既然知道特朗普会撕毁协议，伊朗人为什么要和他签署任何协议呢？
https://prospect.org/2026/07/10/aftermath-wars-on/
去年圣诞节，我在汉堡发表了一场关于“后美国互联网”的演讲，指出世界其他国家现在有机会建立这种互联网，因为特朗普已经将他们过去通过遵守美国科技政策规则所获得的价值清零，尽管特朗普同时将美国科技公司武器化，用来攻击那些反对其议程的各国官员：
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition
在那次演讲之后，我写了一本书（《后美国互联网》），将由 Farrar, Straus and Giroux 于2027年8月出版。在书中，我描述了“可信第三方”（T3P）在复杂交易中扮演的角色。想象一下托管代理人，他们保管着你从卖家那里购买房屋的契约，直到你交钱，然后再将契约转交给你，将钱转交给卖家。

交易越复杂，就越需要 T3P。在过去一个世纪的大部分时间里，美国一直是世界的 T3P。世界上大多数跨洋光缆都在美国登陆，并在美国的数据中心内相互连接。世界上大多数国际交易都以美元进行，并通过 SWIFT 等美国控制的平台进行清算。通过其援助计划，美国为数十亿非美国人制定了医疗和公共服务议程，并且美国在100多个国家设有军事设施。美国训练世界各国的军队，向世界各国的情报机构提供（或隐瞒）信息，并运行着为世界各国政府机构和关键基础设施（从拖拉机到医疗设备）提供动力的 IT 基础设施。
从一开始，美国就从来不是一个完全值得信赖的“可信第三方”。有很多时候，美国滥用其对“中立”平台的控制权，以牺牲依赖这些平台的国家为代价，来服务于美国的国家利益。
但这些违规行为要么是秘密进行的，要么是在某种法律框架（“基于规则的国际秩序”）下实施的。如果一个托管代理人遵守法院命令，在交出地契后扣留资金，你可能还会继续信任他。即使该托管代理人在没有法院命令的情况下，仅凭地区检察官或警长的一句话就扣留资金，这种信任可能依然存在。如果托管代理人有时说：“我要把这笔钱扣留72小时，因为我觉得这笔交易可能有点不对劲。”你甚至可能还会继续信任他。
那个与当地土地登记处和房地产经纪人有着秘密副业的托管代理人也是如此，这种关系让他们能从每笔交易中抽成，并通过空壳公司囤积最好的房产。只要你永远不知道这件事，你就会很乐意雇佣那个托管代理来处理你的房产交易。
特朗普就是那个扣留了钱和地契的托管代理人，然后宣布他这么做是因为卖家是芬太尼毒贩，买家是蜥蜴人；接着他在 Truth Social 上发表了一篇长篇大论，把所有批评他的人都称为恐怖分子，并承诺下次还会这么做。
即使你需要卖房子，即使特朗普是你能找到的唯一托管代理人，你也不会把你的地契或钱交给他。正如 GW Bush 所说：“骗我一次，是你的耻辱……骗我——你不能再骗我了。”
回到 Quiggin 的观点：美国曾是世界上不可或缺的国家，而历史的墓地里埋葬着许多不可或缺的国家。正如 Quiggin 所写，欧洲和乌克兰在很大程度上已经放弃了美国对俄罗斯的军事保护，正在建立自己的能力，在无人机和火炮能力上已经超过了美国。美国再也无法可靠地提供导弹和反导防御了，尤其是在特朗普在伊朗那场毫无意义、无休止的战争中耗尽了美国的库存之后。
Quiggin 指出，反对欧盟成为军事强国的共识认为，欧洲“缺乏在全球投射力量的能力”，而且“过于分裂，无法有效行动”。根据 Quiggin 的说法，只有当你相信后美国时代的军事秩序看起来和运作起来会像特朗普刚刚摧毁的美国体系时，这些才重要。特朗普有一个右翼民粹的“战争部长”，他绑架外国领导人，却无法可靠地让石油通过霍尔木兹海峡——如果这就是“团结”和“投射力量”的红利，那还是留给你自己吧。
在金融方面，Quiggin 指出，欧盟正在竞相打破对 SWIFT、Visa 和 Mastercard 的依赖，特朗普越是将这些工具武器化来对付 International Criminal Court 等机构，这种转型就会越快。
美国那些承担重任的私营机构——比如四大会计师事务所和债券评级机构——已经自我毁灭了，这要归咎于历届美国政府几十年来在接连不断的丑闻中监管松懈。Quiggin 指出，没有理由用值得信赖的版本来取代这些庞大、在结构上举足轻重（却极其不可靠）的垄断联盟。重建我们的经济，使其不再服务于金融体系，让金融回归“其在20世纪70年代以前作为实体经济相对有限服务提供者的角色”，这样成本更低，也更稳健。
在制造业方面，Quiggin 指出了特朗普混乱的关税政策和中国“经济民族主义”这两个并存的事实，它们将欧盟置于新贸易秩序的中心。在这里，我们同样迎来了新事物，既不是欧洲版的“WTO 失败的全球化梦想”，也不是“特朗普试图通过双边欺凌来榨取顺差”：
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/12/opinion/america-trump-nato-europe-world.html
正如我所说，自从上周读了 Quiggin 的文章后，它就一直在我脑海中挥之不去，但在一个方面我认为 Quiggin 弄错了：构建后美国时代互联网的相对难度。
首先，因为 Quiggin 说真正的挑战在于构建后美国时代的 AI。坦率地说，主权 AI 简直是无稽之谈。如果特朗普关掉你们国家所有的聊天机器人，什么都不会改变。如果特朗普命令 Microsoft 切断你们国家对 Office 365 的访问权限（就像他对国际刑事法院和一位惹怒他的巴西法官所做的那样），你们的国家将直接陷入瘫痪：
https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/18/their-trillions-our-billions/#eyes-on-the-prize
如果特朗普命令 John Deere 让你们国家所有的拖拉机变砖，你们就会饿死：
https://pluralistic.net/2022/05/08/about-those-kill-switched-ukrainian-tractors/
面对这些真实的、非推测性的、迫在眉睫的严重威胁，将注意力集中在 AI——这项人类历史上最烧钱、且表现始终不及其鼓吹者承诺的技术——上，纯粹是误入歧途。如果你真的想为你的国家制定一项“AI 战略”，应该是这样的：等待泡沫破裂，然后在随之而来的破产潮中以跳楼价购买硬件和人才，并利用它们从免费的开源模型中榨取更多性能。
真正的数字挑战在于构建应用程序和数据中心，以运行日常的行政、电信和电子商务软件，然后将你们国家、各部委、企业和家庭的数据迁移到这些新平台上。硬件和软件具有挑战性，但最终是直截了当的。为数据中心筹集资金只是说服人们投资做一种“房东”的问题，这是相对容易推销的（而且有很多投资者正在寻找真正的替代方案，以免被卷入 AI 泡沫）。
开发这些应用程序很难，但有一大批技术专家已经准备好迎接更多挑战，他们几十年来一直在为大型科技公司的“收购式雇佣”做虚假创业，和/或为了提高广告点击率而苦干。这些人渴望遵循 Steve Jobs 的教诲去“在宇宙中留下印记”，而他们正被那些想把他们送到萨尔瓦多奴隶劳工营的 ICE 恶棍赶出硅谷。
这里有充足的人才和资本可供获取。
真正的难点不在于编写或运行代码，而在于提取数据、替换固件，以及将新系统（比如后美国时代的社交媒体平台）桥接到现有系统中。这部分之所以困难，是因为世界上每个国家都和美国达成了贸易协议，同意将逆向工程美国技术出口产品定为非法，以换取免关税进入美国市场的机会。特朗普比我更有力地阐述了放弃这些协议的理由：
